Disclaimer on the title slide: "Open AI Codex with Sol 6.1 was used to generate parts of the text, examples and image on slide 17." (OpenAI Codex, Sol 6.1 is listed as a co-author.)

The big picture

This lecture is less about how to build AI than about how an engineer should use it. It starts with what the tools are: artificial intelligence is the umbrella, machine learning fits a model's parameters to examples (training), checks them on separate data (evaluation) and then applies them to new inputs (inference); classification is one such task, done from features to a label. A large language model (LLM) is the same idea applied to text: it is trained on tokens and generates by next-token prediction — which is exactly why it can produce a hallucination: the most likely continuation is not necessarily the true one. The middle of the lecture is about where the model runs (a local model on your machine vs cloud AI on someone else's servers, and AI agents that chain model and tools) and what that means for your data. The last part turns this into rules for study: course rules decide what is allowed (this course's exam: closed-book, no AI), every use is recorded in an AI-use disclosure, a good prompt gives the model what it needs, and every answer — especially an engineering one — is checked by you.

Connection

Lecture 10 of the 25W numbering, 10 Introduction to AI, covers the inside of these models in much more depth: the history of AI, neural networks, CNNs, RNNs, transformers and self-attention, supervised and reinforcement learning, and AI in robot perception. This lecture assumes none of that detail; read it alongside if you want to know what "weights" and "layers" actually are.

Topics

  • What AI is, and how machine learning and LLMs work
  • AI companies and model families
  • Local models, cloud services and Academic AI
  • AI in homework, exams and theses
  • Useful prompting and responsible engineering judgement

What is artificial intelligence?

  • AI systems perform tasks such as perception, prediction and planning.
  • Machine learning fits model parameters using examples.
  • Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple layers.
  • Large language models (LLMs) generate and process language.
Intuition

The four bullets are nested, each a special case of the one before. Artificial intelligence is any system doing a task we would call intelligent (perceiving, predicting, planning) — including hand-written rules. Machine learning is the subset where the behaviour is not hand-written but learned: the program has adjustable numbers (parameters, also called weights) and an algorithm tunes them until the outputs match known examples. Deep learning is machine learning where the model is a neural network with many layers. LLMs are deep-learning models trained on huge amounts of text. So: every LLM is deep learning, every deep-learning model is machine learning, all of it is AI — not the other way round.

Machine learning: training and prediction

Example: predicting a spring's force from its extension.

  • Training compares predictions with known examples.
  • The model adjusts parameters to reduce its error.
  • Evaluation uses separate data to check what the model learned.
  • Inference applies the trained model to a new input.
ExtensionForce
0 mm0 N
5 mm10 N
10 mm20 N
F \approx kx, \qquad k \approx 2\ \text{N/mm}

Idealised teaching data.

Symbols
  • F — force the spring exerts, predicted by the model (N)
  • x — extension of the spring from its rest length (mm)
  • k — spring constant: the model's single parameter, the one number training adjusts (N/mm); the slide's trained value is k \approx 2\ \text{N/mm}
  • \approx — "approximately": the model is a fit to data, not an exact law
Intuition

This is Hooke's law turned into a learning problem. The form of the model (F = kx, a straight line through the origin) is chosen by the engineer; the value of k is what is learned. Training = "find the k that makes the predictions match the table"; inference = "use that k for an extension that is not in the table". A neural network is the same idea with millions or billions of ks instead of one.

Worked example — the four stages on the spring model
  1. Training — measure the error for a candidate k: with the sum of squared errors E(k) = \sum_i (k x_i - F_i)^2 over the three table rows, k = 1.5 gives E = 31.25\ \text{N}^2, k = 2.5 also gives E = 31.25\ \text{N}^2, and k = 2 gives E = 0.
  2. Training — adjust the parameter to reduce the error: the best fit for a line through the origin is k = \sum_i x_i F_i / \sum_i x_i^2 = (5 \cdot 10 + 10 \cdot 20)/(5^2 + 10^2) = 250/125 = 2\ \text{N/mm}.
  3. Evaluation — test on data the model has not seen: a separately measured point, say x = 8\ \text{mm}, F = 16.4\ \text{N}, is predicted as 2 \cdot 8 = 16\ \text{N} — an error of 0.4\ \text{N}. Only this kind of check tells you how well the model generalises; the training rows will always look good, because k was tuned on them.
  4. Inference — use it: a new extension of 7.5\ \text{mm} gives F \approx 2 \cdot 7.5 = 15\ \text{N}.

(x_i, F_i are the extension and force in table row i; E is in \text{N}^2.)

Common mistake

"The model fits the training data perfectly, so it works." A model can match its training examples exactly and still be wrong on new inputs — it may have memorised them, or the real system may behave differently outside their range (a real spring stops obeying F = kx when over-stretched; this model would happily predict 200 N at 100 mm). That is why evaluation uses separate data, and why a model should not be trusted outside the range it was trained on.

Machine learning: classification

Body weight (kg) against body height (cm) for jockeys, basketball players and sumo wrestlers, plus one new person to classify. Invented teaching data: OpenAI Codex, 19 October 2026.

  • Features: height and body weight.
  • Label: occupation.
  • New person: 183 cm, 82 kg — which class?
Intuition

Classification is machine learning where the output is a category, not a number. Each example is described by its features (the measured inputs — here the two coordinates of a point) and carries a label (the right answer — here the occupation, shown as the marker shape). Training learns how regions of feature space map to labels; inference places the new point and reads off its region. The spring example on the previous slide is the other basic task, regression: there the output (a force) is a number.

Worked example — classifying the new person by nearest neighbour

One of the simplest classifiers: give the new point the label of the closest training example. (The slide does not name a method; this is one standard choice. Coordinates below are read off the chart, so they are approximate.)

  1. Write the new point in feature space: (183\ \text{cm},\ 82\ \text{kg}).

  2. Find the closest example of each class (straight-line distance in the plot's units):

    • basketball player at about (188, 85): \sqrt{5^2 + 3^2} \approx 5.8
    • jockey at about (170, 57): \sqrt{13^2 + 25^2} \approx 28.2
    • sumo wrestler at about (172, 138): \sqrt{11^2 + 56^2} \approx 57.1
  3. Take the label of the nearest one: basketball player.
  4. Sanity-check the answer: the new person is on the short, light edge of the basketball cluster — the classifier is confident only because it has three options. See the mistake below.
Common mistake

"The classifier said basketball player, so the person is a basketball player." A trained classifier can only answer with the labels it was trained on. 183 cm and 82 kg is an entirely ordinary adult; the honest answer is "none of these three", but this model has no way to say that. It will always pick some class, however far the input lies from all of them. The same thing happens with every ML model, including LLMs: a confident output says nothing about whether the question was inside what the model knows.

LLMs and next-token prediction

  • Tokens are chunks of text, such as words or parts of words.
  • Training adjusts model weights using many text examples.
  • Generation predicts a next token, adds it to the context and repeats.

Context: "The robot picked up the …"

Next tokenProbability
cube40%
tool30%
part20%
other tokens10%

Illustrative probabilities, not model measurements.

A likely continuation can still be factually wrong.

Intuition

Next-token prediction is autocomplete, done extremely well. Given the text so far (the context), the model outputs a probability for every possible next token; one is picked (usually one of the likely ones), appended to the context, and the whole step repeats — token by token — until the answer is finished. Nothing in this loop looks anything up or checks a fact: "likely" means "similar to how text like this usually continues in the training data". Training is the same as for the spring: compare the predicted next token with the one that actually came next in real text, and nudge the weights to make it more probable.

Why can a fluent LLM answer still be wrong?

Because the model was trained to make text probable, not true. For most common questions the most probable continuation and the correct one coincide, because the training text mostly contained correct statements. But for a rare fact, a specific number, a reference or an exact API name, many plausible-looking continuations have similar probability, and the model has no internal step that tells "I remember this" apart from "this sounds right". It produces a well-formed answer either way, in the same confident tone. That is the mechanism behind the next slide.

AI companies and model families

DeveloperModel family
AnthropicClaude
DeepSeekDeepSeek
GoogleGemini
MetaLlama

Alibaba CloudQwen
OpenAIGPT

Company (developer), model and application are different things.

Intuition

Three layers that are easy to blur: the developer is the company that trains models (e.g. OpenAI); a model is one specific trained set of weights with a name and version (one member of the GPT family); an application is the product you actually type into (a chat website, a coding assistant, a university portal), which may use one or several models and adds its own features and data rules. When you document AI use, or ask "where does my data go?", the answer depends on all three — which is why the disclosure slide asks for tool, provider and model/version.

Hallucinations

  • A hallucination is an output that sounds plausible but is false or unsupported.
  • Examples include invented references, incorrect facts and nonexistent APIs.
  • Missing context and requests for exact details can increase the risk.
  • Sources and tools can help, but their results still need checking.

A confident explanation is not a verification result.

Common mistake

"It gave a detailed explanation and a citation, so it must be right." Detail and confidence are properties of the text, and an LLM produces fluent, detailed text whether or not it is correct (see Why can a fluent LLM answer still be wrong? above). An invented reference typically has a realistic author, journal and year. The only check that counts is an independent one: find the reference yourself in a library database, run the code, redo the calculation, look the value up in the datasheet.

Checking an engineering answer

A planar robot arm with freely rotating joints.

Known quantityValue
First link length0.40 m
Second link length0.30 m
Target positionx = y = 0.75 m

Invented assistant response: "The total reachable length in a single direction is 0.4 m + 0.3 m = 0.7 m. The target is not reachable."

Which check is missing?

Does it work now?

Known quantityValue
First link length0.40 m
Second link length0.30 m
Target positionx = y = 0.60 m
Connection

This is the reachability condition of the two-link arm from 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics (inverse kinematics, Why can a target have zero, one or two solutions?): the tip can only be at a distance r from the base with \lvert d_1 - d_2 \rvert \le r \le d_1 + d_2.

Worked example — answering both slides (the slides leave the answers to the lecture)

With link lengths d_1 = 0.40\ \text{m}, d_2 = 0.30\ \text{m} (notation of 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics):

  1. State the reach of the arm: outer radius d_1 + d_2 = 0.70\ \text{m}, inner radius \lvert d_1 - d_2 \rvert = 0.10\ \text{m}. The workspace is the ring between them.
  2. The missing check — compute the target's distance from the base, not its coordinates:
r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}

For x = y = 0.75\ \text{m}: r = \sqrt{0.75^2 + 0.75^2} \approx 1.06\ \text{m} > 0.70\ \text{m} → not reachable. The assistant's conclusion happens to be right, but it never compared the reach with the target's distance, so its reasoning does not justify it — and the same reasoning would fail on the next case.

  1. Second slide, x = y = 0.60\ \text{m}: each coordinate is now below 0.70\ \text{m}, which tempts "yes, reachable". But r = \sqrt{0.60^2 + 0.60^2} \approx 0.85\ \text{m} > 0.70\ \text{m} → still not reachable. On the diagonal x = y the arm reaches at most x = y = 0.70/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.49\ \text{m}.
  2. Check with a reachable case: x = y = 0.45\ \text{m} gives r \approx 0.64\ \text{m}, inside the ring; the inverse-kinematics formula gives \cos\theta_2 \approx 0.646 (a valid value, \lvert\cos\theta_2\rvert \le 1), so \theta_2 \approx \pm 49.8^\circ, and forward kinematics with \theta_1 \approx 23.9^\circ, \theta_2 \approx 49.8^\circ returns (0.45, 0.45).
Symbols
  • r — straight-line distance from the arm's base (first joint) to the target (m)
  • x, y — target coordinates in the base frame (m)
  • d_1, d_2 — lengths of the first and second link (m)
  • \theta_1, \theta_2 — joint angles; \theta_2 measured relative to link 1, as in 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics (degrees)
Common mistake

Comparing each coordinate with the arm's reach. Reach limits the distance from the base, \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, not x and y separately; a target can have both coordinates under 0.7 m and still be 0.85 m away. The other half of the check is easy to forget too: a target closer than \lvert d_1 - d_2 \rvert = 0.1\ \text{m} is unreachable as well. An assistant (or a person) that skips these checks can be right by accident, as on the first slide — which is why you check the reasoning, not just the verdict.

Local AI models

  • Downloaded model weights run on your own computer.
  • Suitable models can run on CPU or use GPU acceleration.
  • Privacy depends on the application, tools and network connections.
  • Memory depends on parameter count, precision and context length.

Example: 8 billion parameters at 4 bits each ≈ 4 GB of raw weights. The runtime and context cache require additional memory.

Intuition

A local model means the weights — the trained parameters — are a file on your disk, and the arithmetic happens on your own CPU or GPU. Nothing about the model has to leave your machine. But "local" is a property of where the model runs, not a guarantee about your data: the application around it may still send telemetry, search the web, or call other services, which is the third bullet.

Worked example — how much memory do the weights need?
  1. Total bits = parameters × bits per parameter: 8 \times 10^9 \times 4\ \text{bit} = 32 \times 10^9\ \text{bit}.
  2. Convert to bytes (8 bit = 1 byte): 32 \times 10^9 / 8 = 4 \times 10^9\ \text{bytes} = 4\ \text{GB} — the slide's value. (In binary units that is about 3.7 GiB, which is what some tools display.)
  3. Same model at 16-bit precision: 8 \times 10^9 \times 16 / 8 = 16\ \text{GB} — four times as much. Reducing the bits per weight (quantisation) is what makes models fit on ordinary laptops.
  4. A 70-billion-parameter model at 4 bit: 70 \times 10^9 \times 4 / 8 = 35\ \text{GB} — beyond most laptops.
  5. Add the overhead: the runtime and the context cache (which grows with context length) come on top, so plan for more than the raw-weight figure.

Running a local model

  • Model repositories: weights, licences and model cards — e.g. huggingface.co.
  • Runtime: software that loads the model and generates outputs — e.g. ollama.com.
  • Interface: terminal, desktop app, coding extension or WebUI.
  • A local-looking interface may still connect to a remote model.
Intuition

Running a model locally takes three separate pieces, and you choose each one: the weights (downloaded from a repository, along with the licence saying how you may use them and the model card describing what the model is and how it was trained), the runtime (the program that does the maths), and the interface (where you type). The last bullet is the trap: a chat window looks the same whether the runtime behind it is on your laptop or on a server abroad — check the settings, not the look.

Cloud AI and data handling

  • The provider runs the model on remote servers.
  • Prompts and uploads leave your device for processing.
  • Training settings, storage and access are separate questions.
  • Personal data remain subject to GDPR and university rules.

Before uploading: who may receive this material, and for what purpose?

Intuition

With cloud AI, everything you type or upload is sent to the provider's computers. "Is my data used for training?" is only one of three questions: how long is it stored, and who can access it (staff, subcontractors, authorities) are separate, and a "don't train on my data" setting answers only the first. Material that is not yours to share — other people's personal data, unpublished results, a company's documents from an internship — is governed by GDPR and university or contract rules regardless of what the tool allows.

AI agents

  • An agent uses a model and tools to work towards a goal.
  • It can inspect a result, choose another step and repeat.
  • Tools may read files, run code or interact with other software.
  • Local and cloud components can appear in the same workflow.

Example: inspect code, propose a repair, run tests, then report the result.

Intuition

A plain chat model answers once. An agent runs in a loop: decide on a step, use a tool, look at the result, decide the next step — like a closed-loop controller, where the "sensor" is the tool output. That makes it more capable (it can test its own code) but also raises the stakes: an agent with tools can change files and run programs, and each tool may send data to a different place.

flowchart LR
  G[Goal] --> P[Model chooses a step]
  P --> T[Tool: read file / run code]
  T --> R[Inspect result]
  R -->|not done| P
  R -->|done| O[Report]
Connection

The agent loop is the same sense → decide → act cycle as the robot control loops of 6 Dynamics & Control and the reinforcement-learning loop in 10 Introduction to AI: an action is chosen, its effect is observed, and the next action depends on what was observed.

aau.academic-ai.at — student access includes basic AI training in Moodle (about 30 minutes).

PossibilitiesLimitations
Explain a difficult conceptAnswers can be incorrect

Limited image upload and generation

AI in homework, exams and theses

  • Course rules determine which uses and tools are permitted.
  • Open-book exams do not automatically permit AI.
  • Introduction to Robotics: closed-book exam, no AI assistance.
  • For reports and theses, agree the permitted scope with the teacher or supervisor.
  • When the rule is unclear, ask before using the tool.
  • You may always be asked to explain what you did in an oral Q/A.
Common mistake

"Open book means I can use anything, including AI." An open-book exam allows the materials the rules name (notes, books); an AI tool is a different kind of aid and needs its own permission. And for this course the question doesn't arise: the exam is closed-book with no AI at all — so everything practised with AI has to be reproducible without it (see Learning with AI below).

Documenting AI assistance

  • Record the tool, provider, model/version and date where available.
  • Describe the task and which parts of the work it affected.
  • Keep relevant prompts and outputs as required by your course.
  • Cite the original evidence for factual claims.
  • Document language editing and other assistance using the required format.

AI-use disclosure and a source citation serve different purposes.

Intuition

An AI-use disclosure says how the work was made — which tool helped with which part — so the reader can judge what is your own contribution. A citation says where a claim's evidence comes from, so the reader can check it. An AI chat is not evidence for a fact (it may be a hallucination), so it cannot replace the citation: if the AI told you a material's yield strength, you cite the datasheet or textbook where you verified it, and also disclose that AI was used.

AI-generated images

AI-generated illustration: OpenAI, via Codex, 19 October 2026.

  • Useful for illustrating ideas.
  • A realistic picture can contain technical errors.
  • It cannot demonstrate that a design works.
  • Record the tool, date and prompt.

Image prompt: "A photorealistic-looking illustration of a small unbranded six-axis industrial robotic arm with a two-finger gripper, holding a plain metal cube above a laboratory workbench. One robotic arm only, full arm and base visible, clean neutral engineering lab with a light grey background. Realistic metal surfaces and restrained cyan accents, clear readable silhouette, soft natural lighting. No people, no logos, no text, no labels, no charts. This image is explicitly a synthetic illustration, not evidence of a real robot or an engineering design. Keep the scene simple with no extra robotic arms or clutter." Landscape 3:2.

Unclear (slides 1, 19)

The title-slide disclaimer and slide 19 both credit the AI-generated image "on slide 17", but the image is on slide 18 ("AI-generated images"); slide 17 is "Documenting AI assistance" and has no image. Most likely the reference was not updated after a slide was inserted.

Example of an AI-use statement

Adaptable example:

"I used [tool, model/version, provider, date] to obtain feedback on my draft and to correct grammar. Appendix A records the prompts and the changes I accepted. I checked the cited sources and calculations myself and take responsibility for the submitted work."

A statement must accurately describe what you actually did.

AI assistance for this lecture: OpenAI Codex, 19 October 2026. Scope: text and examples. Image credit on slide 17.

Prompting: information the model needs

  • State the task and the relevant background.
  • Provide known values with units and assumptions.
  • Include your attempt, evidence or relevant excerpt.
  • Specify the kind of help and output you want.
  • Ask the assistant to identify missing information before calculating.

A clearer prompt reduces ambiguity. The answer still needs checking.

Why does a more specific prompt give better answers?

Because the model can only continue the context it is given (next-token prediction). Every fact missing from the prompt — the speed, the angle, the assumptions, the level you are studying at — has to be guessed by the model, and a guess is filled with whatever is most typical in its training data, not with what holds in your problem. Supplying the values removes the guessing; asking it to list missing information first turns a silent guess into a visible question. It does not remove the possibility of an error in the reasoning itself — hence the second sentence of the slide.

Prompting example: projectile motion

Vague promptSpecific prompt for learning
"A ball is thrown and lands somewhere. What is its velocity? Please explain.""I am studying introductory mechanics. A ball launches at 20 m/s and 30° above horizontal, and lands at the launch height. Ignore air resistance. Use g = 9.81 m/s². My attempt: vx = 20 cos 30°, vy = 20 sin 30°. Check my setup. Give one hint, then wait. After I try, check flight time, peak height and range, with units."

Which information is missing? (from the vague prompt)

Worked example — what the vague prompt leaves out, and checking the answer yourself
  1. List the missing information (everything the specific prompt adds): launch speed (20 m/s) and angle (30°), landing height (same as launch), the assumption of no air resistance, the value of g, which velocity is wanted (at launch, at the top, at landing?), the student's level and own attempt, and what kind of help is wanted (one hint, not a full solution).
  2. Components (the student's setup — correct): v_x = 20\cos 30^\circ \approx 17.32\ \text{m/s}, v_y = 20\sin 30^\circ = 10.0\ \text{m/s}.
  3. Flight time (vertical motion, back to launch height): T = 2v_y/g = 2 \cdot 10.0 / 9.81 \approx 2.04\ \text{s}.
  4. Peak height (vertical velocity zero at the top): h = v_y^2/(2g) = 100/19.62 \approx 5.10\ \text{m}.
  5. Range (constant horizontal velocity for time T): R = v_x T \approx 17.32 \cdot 2.04 \approx 35.3\ \text{m}.
  6. Check units and plausibility: (\text{m/s})/(\text{m/s}^2) = \text{s} ✓, (\text{m/s})^2/(\text{m/s}^2) = \text{m} ✓; by symmetry the ball lands at 20 m/s, 30° below horizontal. These are the numbers you would use to check whatever the assistant tells you.

(v_x, v_y: horizontal and vertical launch velocity, upward positive; g = 9.81\ \text{m/s}^2; T flight time; h peak height above launch; R horizontal range.)

Learning with AI

  • Attempt the task yourself first.
  • Request feedback or one hint.
  • Explain the corrected solution in your own words.
  • Solve a new variant without assistance.

Could you solve a similar problem tomorrow without the assistant?

Why attempt first and ask for only one hint, instead of the full solution?

Reading a finished solution feels like understanding — every step looks obvious — but it trains recognition, not recall. The exam (closed-book, no AI) tests whether you can produce the steps. Attempting first shows you exactly where you get stuck; one hint fixes that point while you still do the rest of the work; explaining the result in your own words and then solving a fresh variant unaided is the test of whether it stuck. The slide's closing question is that test.

Recommendations

  • Use AI for targeted questions and feedback on your own attempt.
  • Compare suggestions with course material and original sources.
  • Check units, assumptions and limiting cases.
  • Test generated code with cases whose results you know.
  • Use a second model to find disagreements, then verify the disputed claim.
Intuition

Each check is an independent test — one that does not rely on the model being right. Units and limiting cases are the classic engineering ones (an arm reach that grows when a link gets shorter is wrong, whatever the explanation says). Known-answer test cases do the same for code: run it on an input where you can compute the result by hand, like the reachable target x = y = 0.45\ \text{m} above. A second model is useful only for finding disagreements: two models agreeing is not proof, because they may share the same wrong pattern from similar training data — the disputed claim still has to be verified at a source.

Recap and questions

  • How do training and inference differ?
  • What does next-token prediction do?
  • How would you check an invented citation or an engineering answer?
  • What changes when a model runs locally rather than in the cloud?
  • What must you clarify and document before using AI in assessed work?
